Madam Vice President, Excellencies, good morning. The 1972 World Heritage Convention broke new ground by recognizing the links between preserving the environment and protecting the heritage of cultural sites. Today, as we attempt to tackle the accelerating devastation caused by climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss, the Convention is more important than ever, particularly for Indigenous peoples. The triple planetary crisis creates acute threats to Indigenous cultures disrupting and destroying long-standing ways of life and beliefs. And many world cultural and natural heritage sites are ancestral indigenous lands, homes to the living cultures and spiritual inspirations of indigenous peoples. Indigenous traditions also offer us all invaluable insights into how to prevent, mitigate, and adapt to ecological harms. For example, The milpa farming system of Maya peoples in Central America and southern Mexico, involving the cultivation of crops that are nutritionally and environmentally complementary, shows how traditional knowledge can help everyone adapt in the face of climate chaos. Work by the World Heritage Committee and States Parties to manage World Heritage sites with a strengthened focus on the rights and participation of Indigenous Peoples has been of outstanding benefit. The conservation of the Laponian area in Sweden, where the Sami participate in management and decision-making and work to preserve the ancient settlements and ecosystems, or the Taos Pueblo in the United States are just two examples. Empowering Indigenous Peoples to fully participate in decision-making, management and governance of such efforts will be vital to meeting a large range of heritage and human rights challenges in years to come. We therefore welcome UNESCO's recent revisions of its operational guidelines for the implementation of the World Heritage Convention. The guidelines now more strongly recognize the need for state parties to uphold the human rights of Indigenous Peoples, including their rights to free, prior and informed consent in all decisions that may affect their lands, their territories and their resources. UNESCO's work to strengthen its policy on engaging with Indigenous Peoples also creates opportunities for their closer cooperation. I want to emphasize the need for States to obtain the free, prior and informed consent of Indigenous Peoples before any site related to their identity and way of life is proposed for recognition on the World Heritage List. We recommend that States and others require evidence of such consent before approving projects. These and other steps to ensure the decision makers uphold the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples will vastly increase the effectiveness of World Heritage protection. The presence and customary practices of Indigenous Peoples have sustained these sites for generations, and they remain essential to protecting them today. Indigenous Peoples also need to share in the benefits of conservation and any tourism activities developed around World Heritage sites. Conservation is strengthened when indigenous peoples are partners and decision makers with their rights, their knowledge, governance systems and economic interests at the center of heritage efforts. For example, in Australia's Kakadu National Park, World Heritage Project is supported by a system in which traditional owners have a majority on the board of management and revenues from tourism are shared. Traditional owners have exercised their majority regarding access to certain areas of the national park and measures to protect both cultural and natural heritage. Where Indigenous peoples' rights are not respected, they must have access to justice and remedy. World Heritage protection should never involve the forced removal of people, their loss of control over lands and territories and resources, restricted access to sacred sites or livelihoods, or the criminalization of spiritual and religious traditions, customs, and ceremonies. Madam Vice President, the protection of humanity's natural and cultural heritage and respect for Indigenous peoples' rights are important and mutually reinforcing goals around the world and for our office. We work extensively to strengthen the capacity of Indigenous representatives and human rights defenders to participate in decision-making. We also contribute to promoting dialogue between Indigenous Peoples, states, UN bodies, and heritage actors. Last December, we convened a consultation on biodiversity and forest stewardship with Indigenous Peoples and others across Southeast Asia to identify ways to better integrate Indigenous knowledge and rights into environmental programs. we have helped low-lying Pacific Island states to protect their cultural heritage as they deal with rising seas by using traditional knowledge to support adaptation to new conditions. For the past two years, the Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples has enabled representatives of Indigenous Peoples to participate in meetings of the World Heritage Committee. We encourage steps to enable Indigenous Peoples to participate more consistently and effectively in all World Heritage Committee processes, and we look forward to working more extensively with the Committee to advance our shared goals. The civic space for discussion and action by all those who seek to safeguard lands, cultures and nature must be protected, and this must include all Indigenous human rights and environmental rights defenders. They work for the rights of all of us. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Vice Chair, distinguished delegates, representatives of Indigenous peoples, dear colleagues. UNESCO has a long-standing commitment to advancing human rights through its mandate in education, culture, science, and communication. This commitment is reflected in UNESCO's support for the implementation of the United Nations system-wide action plan on indigenous peoples and its efforts to strengthen right-based approaches across its programs. In recent years, the relationship between cultural and natural heritage, human rights, and sustainable development has become an increasingly important area of engagement across the United Nations system. This evolution is reflected in the recent proclamation of the International Decade of Culture for Sustainable Development, 2027-2036, which recognizes that cultural diversity, indigenous knowledge systems, living heritage, and sustainable stewardship practices are essential contributors to resilient societies and sustainable development. Today's discussion is a welcome reflection of this broader evolution and of the growing recognition that culture, nature and people cannot be addressed in separate compartments. Allow me to begin with a simple observation. Across UNESCO-designated sites, including World Heritage properties, biosphere reserves and UNESCO Global Geoparks, it is estimated that at least one quarter overlap with Indigenous Peoples' lands and territories. Many of these places recognized today as part of humanity's heritage are therefore not empty spaces or isolated conservation areas. They are living territories that have been shaped, inhabited, managed, and cared for by communities over generations. The Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted by UNESCO General Conference in 1972 to identify, to protect, and to transmit to future generations cultural and natural heritage of outstanding universal value. One of its greatest strengths, as it has just been recalled, lies in bringing culture and nature together within a single normative international framework. The fact that this discussion is taking place today within the Human Rights Council reflects a growing recognition that heritage conservation and the rights, knowledge system, and cultural value of Indigenous peoples are closely interconnected. This reality points to an increasingly important lesson. The effective safeguarding of heritage depends not only on laws, institutions, or on technical expertise, but also on the experience, the traditions, the custodial practices of the people whose lives remain connected to these places. The implementation of the Convention has evolved significantly in response both to broader developments within the United Nations system and to the engagement of Indigenous Peoples themselves through UNESCO, through the World Heritage Committee, through the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on World Heritage and United Nations human rights mechanisms. At the same time, it is important to recall that the Convention is an intergovernmental treaty. Its policies and procedures are shaped through decisions adopted by State Parties within its governing bodies, particularly the Committee and the General Assembly. The developments discussed today therefore reflect an ongoing process through which State parties have progressively explored how the rights, perspectives and values of Indigenous Peoples can be more effectively reflected in the implementation of the Convention. Significantly, this panel originates from a proposal of the Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, which called not only for greater recognition of Indigenous Peoples' rights in the implementation of the Convention, but also of their values. This distinction is important. It reflects a growing understanding that effective conservation depends not only on protecting places, but also on recognizing the worldviews, practices, spiritual relationships, and custodial traditions through which many of those places have been sustained over generations. From today's perspective, one of the most significant evolutions of this convention has been the growing recognition that what we consider the common heritage of humanity often arises from the care, experience, knowledge, and values of diverse peoples, including Indigenous peoples. Indeed, an important milestone was the addition to the Convention of a fifth strategic objective in 2007, communities. Since then, the Convention has moved beyond a predominantly site-centered and expert-driven approach towards one that recognizes communities and Indigenous peoples as custodians, knowledge holders, and partners in understanding heritage and its conservation. This evolution is consistent with UNESCO's policy on engaging with Indigenous Peoples and with the objectives of the International Decade of Indigenous Languages. For many Indigenous Peoples, language, culture, nature and territory are inseparable. Indigenous languages are repositories of environmental knowledge, memory and customary practices that are often essential to the conservation of both heritage and biodiversity. And this is an understanding that has progressively influenced implementation of the Convention over the past decade. Important milestones have included the adoption of the policy for the integration of a sustainable development perspective into the processes of the Convention, the establishment of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on World Heritage, and the strengthening of reference to consultation, cooperation, and free, prior, and informed consent in the Operational Guidelines. Most recently, the World Heritage Committee has initiated discussions on how Indigenous peoples' heritage values and narratives may be more effectively reflected throughout the Convention processes including nominations, statements of outstanding universal value, management systems and governance arrangements. This direction has also been welcomed by the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues at its last session, which expressed its interest in supporting the implementation of the Committee's decision and participating in future discussions concerning Indigenous peoples' engagement with this Convention. Underlying this discussion is an increasingly important recognition Many challenges arise not only from insufficient participation, but also from the fact that Indigenous conceptions of heritage are not always fully reflected in existing approaches. The question is therefore not only who participates, but also how heritage is understood, interpreted, and presented. These developments are increasingly evident in nomination processes. A number of examples have already been quoted, but let me also quote Pimashowin Aki in Canada, which remains one of the most compelling examples of an Indigenous-led World Heritage nomination. Developed through the leadership of the Anishinaabe First Nations, it demonstrates that Indigenous stewardship systems can themselves form an integral part of a property's heritage significance. These examples reflect an important shift in the implementation of the Convention. Indigenous peoples, as it was just recalled, are increasingly recognized not merely as beneficiaries of conservation outcomes, but as rights holders, knowledge holders, and essential partners in the identification, protection, and management of heritage. At the same time, progress should not obscure ongoing challenges. The World Heritage Convention does not operate in a vacuum. It cannot by itself resolve historic grievances, determine land right, or address all the complexities of relationships between Indigenous peoples and states. Many concerns raised with World Heritage processes reflect broader issues that long predate a nomination or an inscription. Existing Convention mechanisms nevertheless remain important. While the Convention does not establish a formal grievance mechanism, it does provide avenues through which serious concerns may be brought to international attention. Information concerning threats to World Heritage property may be transmitted to UNESCO by sources other than the State Party concerned, and such information is examined through the Convention-established monitoring and reporting processes, including by the World Heritage Committee. These provisions provide an important means of ensuring that concerns can be heard and considered at the international level. Yet, experience demonstrates that prevention is more effective than remediation. Recent reforms, including the preliminary assessment process, provide opportunities to identify issues relating to governance arrangements, right holders, participation and Indigenous Peoples' engagement at an early stage, before positions become entrenched and disputes emerge. Allow me to conclude. More than 50 years after its adoption, the World Heritage Convention continues to evolve in response both to developments within the United Nations system and to the growing engagement of Indigenous Peoples themselves. One lesson has become very clear. Many places recognized today for their outstanding universal value have been sustained through generations of Indigenous stewardship, knowledge, cultural practice, and governance traditions. The continuing evolution of the Convention is not only about expanding participation, it's also about ensuring that these contributions, Indigenous Peoples' contributions, are more fully recognized and reflected through its implementation. The trajectory is therefore clear. Conservation is strongest when it is grounded in partnership, dialogue, and mutual respect. The challenge before all of us, Member States, Indigenous Peoples, UNESCO, and the wider United Nations system, is not only to conserve those exceptional places, it is to ensure that conservation approaches reflect the living relationships between people, culture, nature and territory that sustain them. And in this endeavor, Indigenous peoples are shaping not only the future of heritage conservation, but also the continuing evolution of the World Heritage Convention. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Vice-President. It's a great honour for me to be here with you. I speak on behalf of the International Indigenous Forum on World Heritage. This is an independent platform through which Indigenous Peoples connect to the World Heritage Convention. The majority of those sites were enlisted without free, prior and informed consent with relevant indigenous peoples, and often without any consultation, despite its impact on our territorial rights, self-determination, cultural continuity and ways of life. When it is done With our full and effective participation and respect for our cultural and collective rights, the conception and management of World Heritage sites can play a positive role for Indigenous Peoples, thus contributing to protect our territories, our cultural heritage and our traditional ways of life in the face of development such as mining activities or infrastructure projects. It can also create trade and employment opportunities for Indigenous Peoples. in the area of tourism or directly in the management and conservation of the site. In some cases, sites were designated precisely on the basis of Indigenous Peoples' initiatives in order to protect ancestral territories or establish new opportunities for ways of life. In 2025, the Committee approved Decision 47 COM 11 that explicitly recognizes the challenges confronted by Indigenous Peoples. when they are developing themselves in the World Heritage system, and requests a comprehensive proposal to address those challenges, which should be presented in the 49th session in 2027. Our Forum is actively working on this proposal alongside UNESCO and advisory bodies. Despite these positive efforts, however, the situation on the ground is radically different. The management of many World Heritage sites continues to be characterized by a lack of respect towards the relationship between Indigenous Peoples and their territories, and a disdain for our World Heritage and sacred sites. Serious violations against the human rights of Indigenous Peoples persist in many sites. Wide-ranging evidence of this was clearly demonstrated in a report drawn up by an independent expert panel established by the World Wildlife Fund in protected areas in Africa and Asia, the majority of which are world heritage sites. Abuses against indigenous peoples included murder, sexual violence, torture, physical aggression, illegal detention and arrest, raids on homes and the destruction and theft of personal possessions. Throughout the history of the convention, indigenous peoples have often raised concerns regarding violations of their rights in the implementation of the convention, not only domestically but also internationally, in terms of the practice of the World Heritage Committee and advisory bodies. Concerns include, among other things, a lack of respect for Indigenous Peoples to self-determination and development and the participation in identification, designation and registration of sites, as well as sidelining them in the management and governance of sites, violations in rights and access and use of our lands, as well as territories and resources and the management of sites, harassment and criminalization of Indigenous Peoples making a traditional use of resources, the violations of the right to equitably share the benefits arising from tourism, and a lack of consultation by evaluation and monitoring missions at the sites. It is therefore possible to identify a pattern of violations against indigenous peoples in some of the sites, as has been widely documented by the special procedures of this Council. In Tanzania, in Ngorongoro, the prohibition of subsistence farming promoted by a voluntary relocation strategy of indigenous communities has led to hunger and food insecurity, which have been documented in the Maasai residents. In Kenya, Bogoria Lake was recorded on the World Heritage List in 2011 without free, prior and informed consent of the Endorhiz people. the same community that had just received a historic ruling in the African Commission concerning their rights to their territory. In Thailand, the Kayan Khrasan forest territory was put on the list in 2021 against the explicit request of the IUCN and UN experts, following persistent failings in obtaining consent by the Karen people and the human rights documented against them. In this regard, the expert mechanism, the Special Rapporteur and the International Expert Workshop, which took place in Geneva in 2024, identified the following priority questions and actions. Firstly, The exceptional universal value of the majority of sites located on Indigenous lands was defined without our participation and without recognition for our cultural interpretations and is based on a Eurocentric distinction between natural and cultural heritage and tangible and intangible heritage, which is incompatible with the holistic perspectives of Indigenous peoples. The expert mechanism urged the Committee to review its criteria for assessing exceptional universal values, so that our own values could be recognised in a full and consistent manner in all sites. Furthermore, we invite a systematic revision of existing world heritage sites in this regard. Secondly, there is an inconsistent and non-systematic application of free, prior and informed consent. This isn't currently a obligatory requirement which is systematically applied when States Party designates sites affecting Indigenous Peoples. Submission files are kept away from public access until sites are on the list. Thirdly, it's impossible to have effective participation of representatives of Indigenous Peoples in the Committee's processes. The rules of procedure do not guarantee representatives of Indigenous Peoples or UN experts the use of the microphone before decisions are adopted. Fourthly, it is important to establish a dedicated human rights mechanism as well as an independent complaints and reports mechanism to generate proper reparation across the entire World Heritage system and to formalize cooperation between the Committee and the United Nations human rights system. Thank you very much.

In conclusion, my delegation reaffirms its support for the One China policy and rejects unfounded allegations and politicized criticism relating to the human rights situation in Xinjiang, Tibet, and Hong Kong. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Belarus. You have three minutes.

Madam Vice-President, we categorically reject the unfounded accusations regurgitated in this hall by the Western delegations against Belarus. In Belarus, there is no persecution on political grounds. Individuals who have committed unlawful activities receive proportional sentences on the basis of judicial decisions. We regret that humanitarian steps to release people who have served their sentences is misinterpreted and exploited by certain countries as grounds for another wave of politicised tirades. We stress that the whole Belarus legislative system functions strictly on the basis of the constitution, ensuring lawfulness, law and order with respect to all citizens located on its territory. Choosing Belarus as a target for accusations on political grounds, the Western countries are trying to draw the attention of the human rights system away from the growing problems in their own backyard. Declaring their commitment to rule of law, the European Union in practice takes steps to suppress dissenting voices, introducing harsh censorship, purging the information space and banning dissenting media on the pretext of preserving sustainability of democracy, a controlled socio-political environment is being created. A hallmark of the cynical approach of the EU is the policy of double standards, which is starkly borne out by the situation in specific member states. Lithuania, worried about confiscation of passports, says nothing about the practice of stripping passports from individuals with dual citizenship on the grounds of threats to national security. Estonia, claiming repression, ignores pressure on NGOs at home and criminal persecution of human rights defenders on trumped-up accusations for having an alternative point of view, a source of human rights violations in France is the national justice system. UN human rights mechanisms have repeatedly drawn attention to the fact that that problem is leading to lengthy prison sentences and, as a result, to systemic overcrowding in prisons and pre-trial detention facilities in Norway and Finland. The UN treaty bodies continue to record discrimination against children and teenagers from migrant families on grounds of language, origin and ethnicity. The joint report by the Belarus and Russian foreign ministries on violations of human rights in certain countries contains numerous other examples of systemic human rights violations in Western countries. We suggest that you do your homework and study this document closely. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Sudan. You have equally three minutes.

Thank you very much, Vice-President. We are exercising our right of reply. Following what the organisation, Organisation for Vie has stated, the statement contained partialised and aggressive criticism of our government and we refute those claims. They are baseless. The Sudanese government and army takes very seriously its responsibility to protect the rights of all citizens in line with international law, without the use of prohibited weapons. We are parties to the nuclear prohibition treaty and the treaty on weapons of mass destruction, and this is why we wholeheartedly refute the allegations of weapons we have used as we have travelled the very challenging road that we have been challenging. We are a wholehearted party of our regional organisation. We have always supported and underpinned peace in the region. Notwithstanding, this organisation has chosen to regurgitate the versions of stories that have not been properly substantiated and have undermined the peaceful management of Sudanese society. Other reports by this organization have also come to light. They have cast light on negative and undermining practices. The rapid support forces have been engaged, in fact, in violations of human rights, and the organization hasn't properly taken into account reports which have published by the HRC itself, which have cast light on these reprehensible practices. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Japan. You have three minutes.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. My delegation would like to exercise its right of reply in response to the statement made by China and North Korea. Regarding matters related to history, every country and region should approach its own past with humility and engage with it sincerely. Japan has done so diligently, and Japan's postwar trajectory as a peaceful nation is a testament to this commitment. With remorse for its past, Japan has firmly upheld the purpose at the principle of the UN Charter and championed freedom, democracy and the rule of law, protected and promoted human rights, thereby continuously contributing to prosperity not only in Asia, but also throughout the world. Regarding the abduction issue, the victims and their family are now well advanced in age, and some of them have passed away. There is no time to lose in resolving the abduction issue, which is a humanitarian issue with a time constraint. We strongly urge North Korea to resolve the abduction issue as quickly as possible. Let me emphasize that the claim and the figure mentioned regarding Japan are groundless and based on factual errors. I thank you, Madam Vice President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Indonesia. Indonesia, you have three minutes.

Madam Vice President, Indonesia exercise the right of reply to the statements delivered by NGO yesterday. Our government remains committed to protecting the displaced populations in Papua provinces, ensuring their safety and basic needs and creating conditions conducive to their safe and sustainable return. Any discussion of displacement must also acknowledge its underlying cause. The brutality of the armed separatist group continue to terrorize civilians, urging them to flee and are today displaced. In the past three months, a logistic driver was shot dead after being forced to hold a separatist flag. Nine women were abducted, with seven remains unknown today. Three civil servants were murdered in broad daylight, in cold blood, while on duty, and an American pilot delivering essential logistics for the locals in a remote area was also shot dead. No one should find these atrocities acceptable, and no one should justify them under any circumstances. Madam Vice-President, on the national strategic project, it is a national initiative to realize the right to development for all people. Amid climate volatility and disruption to global supply chain, this initiative is critical to strengthen food security, create employment, and expand economic opportunities. In Papua provinces, the projects are also aimed at accelerating the regional development in line with Papua's special autonomy framework, prioritizing improved welfare of the Papuans. The implementation involves coordination and consultations with local authorities and civil society, while considering spatial planning, environmental protection, cultural heritage, as well as the rights and interests of other communities. Vice Presidents, finally, on impacts of current economic and development models on women, Indonesia believe development and human rights must advance together. Women should participate meaningfully in decision making and benefit equally from development, contributing to poverty eradications and to people's welfare. We note that the constitutional review of the job creation law also demonstrate an available and functioning legal avenue to challenge public policies. We do not condone excessive use of force and unequivocally condemns violence against women, including sexual violence. Our law on sexual violence crimes provides protections, access to justice and remedies for victims. For us, women are and will remain central agents of our democracy and development. We remain firmly committed to protecting their rights, participation and freedom from violence. I thank you, Madam Vice President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Iran. You have three minutes.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. My delegation would like to exercise this right of reply in response to use of the false designation for the Persian Gulf by certain delegation. The Islamic Republic of Iran firmly rejects that terminology. The name of this body of water is not a matter of political interpretation. It is an established geographical name rooted in history and consistently reflected in authoritative maps, geographical works, navigational charts, and official documents over centuries. The established name is the Persian Gulf. The United Nations has, over the case, maintained the established designation Persian Gulf in its official document publications. UN practice cannot be replaced by unilateral political preferences or by terminology introduced for political purposes. Iran has repeatedly raised this matter through the appropriate diplomatic and institutional channels, including in relation to the United Nations publications where inconsistent terminology has appeared. Such usage should be corrected in accordance with the established UN terminology and editorial practice. The Islamic Republic of Iran calls upon all delegations to respect the established geographical nomenclature and to refrain from introducing false terminology into the official discourse of the United Nations. The name is clear, established, and internationally recognized: the Persian Gulf. I thank you, Madam Vice-President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Cuba. You have three minutes.

Madam Vice President, the key person in Tatoofu is Tatoofu, the eponymous protagonist, a person who presents himself as holding great values, but there is a consistency between what the eponymous protagonist promotes and reality. Attributing a moral authority to him, other characters have clearly lost their way. We can see in this room what happens when policies of systemic discrimination are well known, that are being applied in the country of other speakers against people. Roma children in the Republic of Czechia are experiencing such discrimination in their classrooms. The European Union has also found that the country is denying basic core services to these people. Migrants and refugees are victims of xenophobia and intolerance. The Czechia representatives must demonstrate more modesty and practice self-awareness and criticism before they assess others. and accuse them of serious violations of human rights when these are occurring in their own country. Vice-President, let us not forget the shameful action of the Republic of Czechia protecting impunity, the impunity of Israel committing atrocities in Gaza and other occupied territories. They have opposed all resolutions aimed at providing any minimal protection to the life and human rights of the Palestinian people. The Republic of Czechia, alongside the United States and Israel, have supported an unacceptable campaign of attacks and pressure against the Special Rapporteur for the Occupied Territories in order to attempt to silence these. We demand that the Republic of Czechia respect the autonomy of independent experts who have been designated by this Council. They feign interest for human rights in Cuba, but they have said not a single word on the criminal embargo by the United States. This collective punishment is killing our women, children and old people, and is flagrantly violating the human rights of the Cuban people. The Republic of Czechia is complying with the precise requests of the US State Department and is entirely silent on this. They are paying total lip service to Washington, and they're not respecting human rights. Cuba doesn't interfere with any country, and it doesn't give lessons to anyone. But we're not going to remain silent in the face of hypocrisy. Thank you very much, Vice President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Cyprus. You have three minutes.

Thank you, Vice-President. The Republic of Cyprus exercises its right to reply in response to yet another attempt by Turkiye to divert this Council's attention from the human rights consequences of its own actions in Cyprus. It is deeply troubling to hear Turkey lecture from this forum on human rights while maintaining a military presence and effective control over the northern part of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus. Cyprus categorically rejects any attempt to present the situation as legitimate or to distort the applicable rules of international law. The facts remain clear. Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 and has since occupied 36.3% of its territory while maintaining substantial military presence in the northern part of the island. The Security Council has repeatedly addressed the consequences of attempted cessations, including through resolutions 541 and 550. The European Court of Human Rights has likewise established Turkey's responsibility for violations arising from its effective control in the northern part of Cyprus. The human consequences of this situation cannot be erased. Thousands of Cypriots were displaced from their homes. Their property rights remain unresolved. Families of missing persons continue to seek answers and closure. The Republic of Cyprus continues to call for full cooperation with the Committee on Missing Persons and for access to information necessary to determine the fate of those who remain unaccounted for. The rights of enclave Greek Cypriots and Maronites have also been affected, including in relation to education, religion, and freedom of expression. At the same time, demographic changes in the occupied area have fundamentally altered the character of communities that existed before 1974. Cyprus has repeatedly raised these concerns regarding settlement policies and their implications under international law. Madam Vice-President, the narrative of the so-called isolation of the Turkish Cypriots cannot be used to obscure the broad reality of the Cyprus problem. The division of the island is not an abstract political disagreement. It has concrete and continuing consequences for the rights of people on both sides. The Republic of Cyprus does not accept that a permanent division is the answer, nor can a two-state arrangement provide a substitute for a settlement based on a bizonal, bicommunal federation with political equality in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions. Cyprus will continue to defend the rights of all its citizens and to seek a comprehensive settlement that reunifies the island and allows both Greek and Turkish Cypriots to live together in security, dignity and equality. What is required is not further rhetoric, but respect for international law and genuine cooperation towards ending the division of Cyprus. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Pakistan. You have three minutes.

Madam Vice President, Pakistan is exercising its right of reply in response to the Indian delegation's baseless remarks. Jammu and Kashmir is not, was not, and never will be an integral part of India. The only integral consideration here is India's brazen disregard for international law and suppression of the right to self-determination of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. Unable to answer for its record of human rights violations, India seeks to hide behind tired tropes of terrorism and hollow promises of development. We reject both India's attempted deflection as well as its absurd allegations. In countering the scourge of terrorism, Pakistan has rendered enormous sacrifices. The international community acknowledges our contributions. India, meanwhile, tries to masquerade as the victim, yet boasts publicly about using terrorism as an instrument of policy. This Council would recall its serving military officer confessed to orchestrating his government's support for terrorist groups in Pakistan's province of Balochistan. Earlier this year, an Indian national pled guilty in a U.S. court to a murder-for-hire plot at the behest of Indian intelligence. In October 2024, less than two years ago, Indian diplomats were expelled from a country in North America for being implicated in homicide, intimidation, and coercion on their host soil. India has no standing whatsoever to hector this Council on terrorism. On Azad Jammu and Kashmir, India's attempted equivalence is categorically false. Azad Jammu and Kashmir has its own constitution, legislature, judiciary and political life. There is no resemblance to Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, where over 900,000 troops and draconian laws have sought to extinguish all human rights and every avenue for accountability or remedy for eight decades. Madam Vice-President, the Hindutva ideology that animates India's conduct operates identically at home and in the territory that it occupies. India's ruling dispensation celebrates the demolitions of mosques, the lynching of Muslims, and the bulldozing of minority homes amidst rhetoric of domination. UN special procedures have documented this climate of hatred and exclusion. And in illegally occupied Jammu and Kashmir is not the only example of the results of this state-sanctioned hatred. In Manipur, for instance, for more than two years, tribal communities have been subjected to systematic violence. The government's complicity is documented, as is the absence of meaningful accountability. Such pursuit of dominance is also the engine of the Indian occupation of parts of Jammu and Kashmir. The suppression of the inalienable rights promised to its people by relevant UN Security Council resolutions and their ongoing cultural erasure through secular colonialism and demographic re-engineering. The self-proclaimed world's largest democracy has become a cautionary tale about the weaponization of majoritarian exclusion. India will not stop trying to silence the people of illegally occupied Jammu and Kashmir. The question is whether this Council would let it. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Lithuania. You have three minutes.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. I am exercising this right of reply in response to the statement made by the delegation of Belarus. We would like to remind that the authorities of Belarus regularly impose forced expulsion as a mandatory condition for some political prisoners' release a practice which violates international human rights law. Just last week, 25 released political prisoners were deported to Lithuania, some of them without passports, while others have reported that their passports were cancelled following their expulsion from Belarus. We continue to be concerned about the fate of at least 884 political prisoners still unjustly detained under appalling conditions in isolation from families and lawyers, subjected to ill treatment and torture with no access to essential health services. We also express our concern about new arrests and re-arrests and restrictions on the rights and freedoms of those who have been released inside Belarus. We consequently reiterate our calls for the immediate and unconditional release of all remaining political prisoners in Belarus, for their effective rehabilitation, and urge the authorities to bring the end to repression. I thank you.
Thank you. I understand that Democratic People's Republic of Korea has requested a second right of reply. You have two minutes.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. I will be brief in exercising my second right of reply. Japan does not have moral grounds to discuss human rights in the international arena. It cannot evade its historical responsibility for the grave crimes committed against humanity. These historical injustices continue to warrant sincere reflection and accountability. Rather than making provocative accusations against other countries, the Japanese delegation would be better advised to approach these issues with humility, engage in honest self-repentance, and demonstrate genuine remorse for the suffering inflicted by its past actions. I thank you.
Thank you. Also, I understand that Turkey wishes to have a second right of reply. You have the floor and you have two minutes.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. We would like to exercise our second right of reply. It is indeed true that there is still an occupation in Cyprus, which is the occupation of the government of the now-defunct Republic of Cyprus by the Greek Cypriots. The 1960 partnership Republic of Cyprus, which was established between the two political equals, namely Turkish Cypriots and Greek Cypriots, has only lasted for three years. In 1963, the Greek Cypriot side resorted to violence, and the Turkish Cypriots were expelled from all organs of the government and even from their homes by force of arms. As a result of this ethnic cleansing campaign directed at Turkish Cypriot people with the ultimate aim of eliminating all the Turkish Cypriots, UN peacekeeping force was deployed in the island in 1964. When they made a final attempt in 1974 through a coup d'etat with the ultimate aim of enosis by eliminating all the Turkish Cypriot people, Turkey as a guarantor power intervened on the island to save the lives of the Turkish Cypriot people. Therefore, it is quite absurd to describe the subsequent presence of the Turkish troops in the island as occupation. Lastly, I would like to recall that none of the UN Security Council resolutions on Cyprus have ever referred to the legitimate intervention of Turkey and the presence of Turkish troops to deter further Greek Cypriot atrocities on the island as occupation. I thank you.
Thank you. I recognize Japan, who has also requested a second right of reply. You have two minutes, madam.

Thank you, Madam Vice Chair, President. My delegation would like to exercise the second right of reply in response to the statement made by China and North Korea. Regarding matter related to history, we will not respond to each of them in detail at this time. For over 80 years since the end of World War II, Japan has consistently upheld democracy and human rights. Japan has consistently pursued the path of a peaceful nation since the end of the war, making contribution to global peace and prosperity and effort to improve human rights. Japan intend to continue contributing peace as a responsible member of the international community. Regarding people from Okinawa, Okinawa prefecture has its own unique and the rich culture and tradition just like other region in Japan. The government of Japan, however, is not of the view that the people born in Okinawa are indigenous people or are part of an indigenous ethnic group, nor is such a view widely recognized in Japan. On the right of immigrant, the right of immigrant are guaranteed the same as the Japanese national according to domestic law. Regarding discrimination against women, Japan has been advancing elimination the discrimination against women. With regard to the abduction issue, Japan continues to strongly urge North Korea to resolve the abduction issue immediately. Finally, let me reiterate that the claim and the figure regarding Japan are groundless and based on factual error. I thank you, Madam Vice President.
Thank you. I would call upon all speakers to uphold UN standards when referring to countries. I understand that also Cyprus wishes to have a second right of reply. You have two minutes, madam.

I am exercising the second right of reply to the statement made by Turkey. Rather than acknowledging its responsibility in the continuing human rights violations in Cyprus and engaging constructively towards ending them, Turkey keeps retorting to a selective interpretation of history to divert attention from the fact that it violates the UN Charter and international law. No amount of disinformation can change certain realities, such as a persistent violation of international law, including the UN Charter and international human rights law. The international community is well aware as to the identity of the occupation power in Cyprus and the responsibilities that emanate from there. The respective judgments by the European Court of Human Rights, which, despite being a Council of Europe member, Turkey refuses to implement, are unequivocal. Turkey was found to have effective control over the areas it occupies in Cyprus. The so-called isolation of the Turkish Cypriot community is due to a single factor, the continuing Turkish occupation, and no amount of protest in this forum can change the fact that Turkey is violating international law, which affects all Cypriots. I thank you.
Thank you. I also recognize China, who wishes to exercise their second right of reply. You have two minutes, sir.

Madam Vice President, China exercise the right to reply regarding to the statement by the delegation of Japan. We exercise our right again. This year is the 80th anniversary of the opening of Tokyo trials. It is raised great concern to know Japanese textbooks continue to downplay characterization of its aggression. Right wing forces even use AI to filter and screen records of the Tokyo trials in attempt to whitewash war crimes and entrench erroneous, wrongful historical perception. This is not only serious regression in understanding of history, but also an organized, politically motivated, pervasive, perversive move. We admonish Japan to do some deep soul-searching, properly address historical issues. Thank you, Madam Vice President.

Thank you. Is there any other delegation wishing to exercise a right of reply? I see none. Excellencies, distinguished participants, with that, we have concluded the consideration of agenda item 4. Distinguished participants, this brings us to the end of this meeting. We will reconvene in the afternoon at 3:00 p.m. to hold the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous Peoples, to be followed by the interactive dialogue on the Secretary-General's report on cooperation with the United Nations. I hereby close the 23rd meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council.
